note: Extracted from three practitioner sources held by this index: SRC-002 (LaValle et al., Peptide Handbook, 2022), SRC-003 (Campbell, Optimize Your Health with Therapeutic Peptides, 2023) and SRC-005 (Hack Smith, The Complete Guide to Peptides, 2025). BPC-157 is the deliberately harder half of this pair. There is no approved product, no human trial in anything held here, and three sources that describe three different regimens. The architecture's job on this record is to keep all of that visible at once without letting volume of discussion read as weight of evidence.

compound.shortDescription: A synthetic fifteen-amino-acid peptide, described by the sources held here as derived from a protein found in human gastric juice. Very widely discussed, almost entirely on animal research: a literature screen identified three small uncontrolled human studies and no approved product anywhere.
compound.simpleSummary:
BPC-157 is a short synthetic peptide. The sources held here describe it as a fragment of a larger protein found in stomach fluid, which is where the name comes from: body protection compound.

It is discussed more than almost any other compound in this field, largely in the context of healing — tendons, ligaments, muscle, gut lining, skin. There is a considerable body of laboratory and animal work behind those claims, and the practitioner sources held here are careful about how they say it: one describes the effects as observed "in laboratory studies".

**Research in people is very limited.** A search of the PubMed medical literature database on 13 September 2026 returned 230 records mentioning the compound. Reading through them, three were studies in people: two people given it intravenously, twelve women given it for a bladder condition, and a review of the records of seventeen patients given it in the knee. Thirty-one people in total, across three studies, none of which had a comparison group. That last point matters more than the numbers. Without a comparison group, a study cannot tell whether the people who got better did so because of the treatment.

Almost everything else is animal research. No medicines regulator has approved BPC-157 anywhere, and the reason two independent reviews give is that the clinical research needed to assess it has not been done.
compound.practitionerSummary:
Synthetic pentadecapeptide, sequence Gly-Glu-Pro-Pro-Pro-Gly-Lys-Pro-Ala-Asp-Asp-Ala-Gly-Leu-Val, MW reported as 1419.556 g/mol, described as a partial sequence of body protection compound isolated from human gastric juice.

Mechanisms reported by the sources held here, all from laboratory work: angiomodulation — described as increasing angiogenesis where needed and decreasing it where not, including in tumour metastasis; nitric oxide stimulation; upregulation of VEGF, FGF and TGF-β; F-actin formation in fibroblasts; increased fibroblast migration and dispersal; increased phosphorylation of paxillin and FAK without change in the amounts produced; upregulation of anti-inflammatory transcription factors and downregulation of TNF-α; upregulation of growth hormone. Additional reported domains: neuroprotection with effects described on serotonergic, dopaminergic, opioid and GABAergic systems; cardioprotection including reported counteraction of neuroleptic-induced QTc prolongation; gastroprotection against ethanol, NSAIDs, corticosteroids, neuroleptics and capsaicin. Topical application reported to accelerate closure after alkali burn via granulation, re-epithelialisation and collagen deposition through ERK1/2.

**What the screen replaced.** This record previously said, under this heading, that no human evidence was held by this index, and noted that a PubMed search had returned 228 records none of which had been read. The screen recorded below read them. Three are human studies, so the earlier statement was true of the library and misleading about the world — which is exactly why it was bounded to the register at the time, and why the screen was the next thing to do.

Pharmacokinetics: nothing. No source held here reports bioavailability, half-life, distribution or elimination for any route.

Routes: subcutaneous and oral are both reported, and one source reports topical in an animal burn model. No source held here compares them, and none reports what fraction of an oral amount is absorbed intact — which for a pentadecapeptide is the question that determines whether an oral route means anything.

Safety, as reported: described as safe in recommended amounts by one source, with caution advised in cancer and other conditions where angiogenesis may need to be suppressed. Rare reactions listed as erythema, transient muscle atrophy, polyarthralgia with hand oedema, and rash. Paediatric safety not established. The angiogenesis caution and the reported anti-tumour effects sit in tension within the same source, and this index records both rather than resolving them.

Regulatory: no approval, no authorisation and no assessment in any jurisdiction, in anything held here.

Protocols: three sources, three different regimens, recorded separately and attributed. None cites a study establishing its amounts.

**Human evidence.** Three primary human studies identified by a PubMed screen on 13 September 2026, all uncontrolled: n = 2 intravenous safety pilot, n = 12 single-procedure injection for interstitial cystitis, n = 17 retrospective intra-articular chart review. No RCT exists.

**Citation crosswalk.** All twenty-two references the practitioner handbook gives for its BPC-157 entry are preclinical or reviews; twenty-one resolve to records in the screen (fourteen animal studies, seven reviews). The sole citation for tumour cell growth inhibition is a 2004 conference abstract in a human melanoma cell line, not indexed in PubMed. The cancer-cachexia claim traces to a 2018 review that states it is written before any clinical trial. A clinician following the handbook's citations will not reach human evidence, because there is none at the end of them.
compound.unknownsSummary:
Whether BPC-157 does anything useful in people. Three human studies have been identified and none of them can answer that, because none had a comparison group — and the conditions they looked at are ones that come and go on their own.

Also unknown: how much, how often, for how long, by which route, what happens on stopping, what happens with prolonged use, whether the material sold under this name is what it says it is, and whether the effect on blood-vessel growth is a hazard in cancer or a therapeutic possibility — a question on which two research groups disagree in print and neither has human evidence.

One more thing is unknown in a different way. A 2006 review states that clinical trials in inflammatory bowel disease were carried out under three development codes. No report of them appears in this search, and a 2026 review states that no Phase II trial has been completed. This index cannot tell whether those trials were run and never published, or whether the characterisation is wrong. It is recorded as a lead.

The volume of discussion around this compound is not evidence, and this record is arranged so that the two are not mistaken for each other.

compound.molecularDescription: Molecular weight reported as 1419.556 g/mol. The molecular formula printed in the held copy is degraded by optical character recognition and is not transcribed rather than transcribed wrongly.
compound.naturalOrSynthetic: Synthetic. The sources describe it as a partial sequence derived from a protein found in human gastric juice; the peptide administered is made synthetically and is not itself isolated from anyone.
compound.nomenclatureNote: The sources held here describe BPC-157 as 'derived from' body protection compound in gastric juice. That is a statement about where the sequence came from, not a statement that the body produces this fifteen-amino-acid peptide. The inference from 'derived from something the body makes' to 'natural, and therefore safe' is common and is not supported by anything here.

claims.claimText: BPC-157 is a synthetic pentadecapeptide with the sequence Gly-Glu-Pro-Pro-Pro-Gly-Lys-Pro-Ala-Asp-Asp-Ala-Gly-Leu-Val, described by the sources held here as a partial sequence derived from body protection compound found in human gastric juice.
claims.plainLanguageText: BPC-157 is a short chain of fifteen amino acids, made synthetically. Its sequence comes from part of a larger protein found in stomach fluid.
claims.interpretationNotes: Two sources agree on the derivation and one gives the sequence explicitly. This index records the derivation as the sources state it — the sequence is derived from a gastric protein — and does not extend that into a claim that the body produces this peptide, which the sources do not say and which is the inference most often drawn from it.
claims.uncertaintyText: Neither source held here cites an isolation or characterisation paper that this index has read. Whether the administered peptide is identical to any naturally occurring fragment is not established by anything held here.

evidence.interpretation: The source gives the fifteen-residue sequence, the molecular weight, and the category 'gastric pentadecapeptide', and lists Body Protection Compound-157 and Bepecin as other names.
evidence.populationModel: Not applicable — a statement about the molecule.

evidence.interpretation: The source describes BPC-157 as a synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide derived from a peptide called body protecting compound produced in stomach acid.

claims.claimText: A PubMed screen conducted on 13 September 2026 returned 230 records and identified three primary human studies of BPC-157, involving 31 people in total. All three are small, uncontrolled, unblinded, single-site and published in the same journal. The remaining evidence identified by the screen is preclinical: 162 animal studies, one human-tissue preparation and two in vitro studies, alongside 48 reviews and 7 commentary pieces.
claims.plainLanguageText: Most of what is said about BPC-157 comes from laboratory and animal research. A search of the medical literature found three studies in people, together involving thirty-one participants. None of them had a comparison group, so none can show that an effect was caused by the compound rather than by anything else.
claims.interpretationNotes: This claim replaces one that said no human study was recorded in the sources held here. That was true of the library and said nothing about the literature, which is why the screen was run. The answer it returned is not the one the register implied: human studies exist. They are also not the kind of evidence that would support any of the uses attributed to this compound — two participants, twelve participants and a seventeen-patient chart review, none controlled, are hypothesis-generating at best. A systematic review published in 2025 searched three databases independently to June 2024 and included 36 studies, of which it classified one as clinical, and reported that it found no clinical safety data. Two independent screens reaching the same shape of answer is worth more than either alone.
claims.uncertaintyText: This is a statement about one database on one date under one set of criteria, and it is bounded to that. PubMed is not the whole of the scientific literature: it indexes neither conference abstracts nor most regulatory submissions, and a 2006 review asserts that clinical trials for inflammatory bowel disease were conducted under the development codes PL 10, PLD 116 and PL 14736 — no report of which appears in this search. Those trials are recorded as a gap, not as evidence and not as absence. All three human studies were read at abstract level; the full texts are not held.

evidence.interpretation: An IRB-approved study of intravenous infusion in two adults over three days, with blood work and vital signs before and after each infusion, reporting no measurable change in the biomarkers tested and no reported side effects.
evidence.populationModel: Two adults at a private clinic, both of whom had received intravenous BPC-157 before the study.

evidence.interpretation: Twelve women with interstitial cystitis who had not responded to pentosan polysulfate, treated during a single cystoscopy with injections around the area of inflammation, with outcome assessed by a self-reported global response questionnaire.
evidence.populationModel: Twelve women aged 39 to 76 at a single private clinic.

evidence.interpretation: A retrospective one-year chart review of seventeen patients given intra-articular BPC-157, alone or combined with thymosin beta-4, followed up by telephone survey with no validated instrument.
evidence.populationModel: Seventeen patients at one clinic; sixteen were reached for follow-up.

evidence.interpretation: An independent systematic review, two screeners, three databases, searched to June 2024: 544 records identified, 36 studies included — 35 preclinical and 1 clinical — and no clinical safety data found.
evidence.populationModel: Not applicable — a review of the literature.

claims.claimText: The healing effects reported in laboratory studies include accelerated wound and tissue healing across tendon, ligament, bone, muscle, skin and gastric mucosa, with reported mechanisms including improved tissue granulation, fibroblast recruitment and collagen formation.
claims.plainLanguageText: In laboratory work, the compound has been reported to speed healing across several tissue types, by encouraging the processes that rebuild tissue.
claims.interpretationNotes: Recorded as a description of what laboratory work has reported, with the tissue list kept as the source gives it rather than generalised to 'healing'. The specific mechanisms named — granulation, fibroblast recruitment, collagen formation — are what the source offers as the how, and are recorded because a mechanism makes a claim checkable in a way that an outcome alone does not.
claims.uncertaintyText: Preclinical, entirely. A result in an animal model is not a result in a person, and a mechanism operating in cell culture is not an effect in a body. The primary papers behind these reports have not been opened by this index, so the models, the doses and the routes used are all unknown here.

evidence.interpretation: The source lists 'Helps heal tissues — promotes microscopic regeneration; improves tissue granulation, fibroblast recruitment and collagen formation' among the effects reported in laboratory studies, with the tissue list given in its opening sentence.
evidence.populationModel: Laboratory studies, models not specified by the source.

evidence.interpretation: The source lists healing of wounds and injuries in muscles, tendons, ligaments, bone and skin, and increased blood flow to damaged areas, as effects consistently observed in animal studies and anecdotal report.

claims.claimText: The sources describe BPC-157 as angiomodulatory rather than simply pro-angiogenic: reported to increase blood vessel formation where needed and decrease it where not, including in tumour metastasis, and to stimulate nitric oxide production and the angiogenic cytokines VEGF, FGF and TGF-β.
claims.plainLanguageText: The sources describe it as adjusting blood vessel growth in both directions rather than only increasing it — including reducing it in the context of tumours.
claims.interpretationNotes: This claim is recorded because of the tension inside it, not despite it. The same source that describes bidirectional angiomodulation and reports inhibition of tumour cell lines also advises caution in cancer and other conditions where angiogenesis may need to be suppressed. Both are recorded, and the tension is recorded as a disagreement on this page rather than resolved by choosing the more reassuring of the two.
claims.uncertaintyText: 'Increased when needed, decreased when needed' is a strong claim and, as stated, an unfalsifiable one: it describes an outcome without a mechanism that would predict which direction occurs when. The source offers no criterion. Nothing held here establishes what determines the direction, or whether the bidirectional behaviour has been observed outside the specific models cited.

evidence.interpretation: The source lists BPC-157 as a 'potent angiomodulatory factor' that 'modulates angiogenesis — increased when needed, decreased when needed such as in tumor metastasis', and separately lists nitric oxide stimulation and the angiogenic cytokines VEGF, FGF and TGF-β.

The source states that despite its ability to promote angiogenesis, BPC-157 is reported to inhibit and counteract increased VEGF expression and subsequent signalling, thus avoiding VEGF-tumorigenesis, and that it inhibits the growth of several tumour cell lines and can counteract tumour cachexia.
evidence.populationModel: Tumour cell lines and laboratory models.

evidence.interpretation: The same source advises using BPC-157 with caution in cancer and other conditions where angiogenesis may need to be suppressed — a caution that sits against its own account of bidirectional angiomodulation and anti-tumour effect.

claims.claimText: The sources held here report both subcutaneous and oral administration, and topical application in an animal burn model, without comparing them or reporting bioavailability for any route.
claims.plainLanguageText: Injection under the skin, swallowing, and application to the skin are all described. No source held here says how much reaches the body by any of these routes, or compares them.
claims.interpretationNotes: Recorded as a claim because the oral route is the one a reader is most likely to act on and the one the sources support least. A fifteen-residue peptide taken orally faces gastric and intestinal proteolysis, and whether any survives intact is precisely the question the sources do not address. This index records that they report the route and records that they establish nothing about it.
claims.uncertaintyText: No bioavailability figure, no pharmacokinetic study, and no comparison between routes appears in anything held here. That an amount is reported for a route is not evidence that the route delivers the peptide. For the oral route in particular, this index holds nothing addressing whether the peptide survives digestion.

evidence.interpretation: The source gives separate subcutaneous and oral amounts under 'Dosage', and lists an available injectable solution strength. It gives no bioavailability figure for either.

The source reports that topical treatment accelerated wound closure following an alkali burn, with a mechanism attributed to granulation, re-epithelialisation, dermal remodelling and collagen deposition through ERK1/2 signalling.
evidence.populationModel: Animal burn model; species not specified by the source.

claims.claimText: The sources held here report no approved product, no regulatory assessment and no approved indication for BPC-157 in any jurisdiction.
claims.plainLanguageText: There is no approved medicine containing BPC-157. No regulator, in anything this index holds, has assessed it for any use.
claims.interpretationNotes: Recorded as an explicit claim rather than as an empty regulatory section, because an empty section reads as 'not yet filled in' and this is a finding. Two of the three sources are practitioner handbooks that name brand names and manufacturers for other compounds — including for tesamorelin in the same volume — and name none here.
claims.uncertaintyText: This is a statement about what the sources held here record. It is not a statement about the regulatory position in any particular jurisdiction, which would require a regulatory source, and this index holds none for this compound. Regulatory status also changes, and the most recent source here is from 2025.

evidence.interpretation: The source's 'Other Name(s)' field for BPC-157 lists only descriptive names and Bepecin, with no brand name, manufacturer or approval — in contrast with the same handbook's tesamorelin entry, which names Egrifta and Theratechnologies.

claims.claimText: Reported adverse effects are limited: one source describes BPC-157 as safe in recommended amounts, listing erythema, transient muscle atrophy, polyarthralgia with hand oedema and rash as rare reactions, and states that paediatric safety has not been established.
claims.plainLanguageText: The handbook describes it as safe at the amounts it recommends and lists a small number of uncommon reactions. It states that safety in children has not been established.
claims.interpretationNotes: Recorded with its provenance foremost. 'Reported safe in recommended dosages' is a statement by a practitioner handbook about amounts that the same handbook recommends, with no study cited for either the amounts or the safety. A short list of adverse effects is what one expects when there is no systematic collection of them, and absence of reported harm is not evidence of safety.
claims.uncertaintyText: No human safety study, no pharmacovigilance record and no systematic adverse-event collection appears in anything this index holds. A compound with no trials has no trial safety data, and a short adverse-effect list from a handbook is not the same thing. Nothing here addresses prolonged use, interactions, or use in any specific population.

evidence.interpretation: The source states that BPC-157 is reported safe in recommended dosages, advises caution in cancer and conditions where angiogenesis may need suppressing, and notes that redness and pain at the injection site may occur.
The source lists rare adverse reactions as erythema, transient muscle atrophy, polyarthralgia combined with hand oedema, and rash, and states that safety in paediatrics has not been established.

claims.claimText: None of the three identified human studies had a control group, a randomisation procedure, or blinding, and all three were conducted at private clinics and published in the same journal. Two of the three used material whose identity and purity are not established in the report: one names a 503A compounding pharmacy as the manufacturer, and one gave a second peptide to part of the cohort.
claims.plainLanguageText: The human studies that exist are small and have no comparison group. That means that if the people in them improved, the study cannot show whether the compound caused it. It is the kind of research that suggests what to test next, not the kind that settles anything.
claims.interpretationNotes: Recorded as a claim of its own rather than as a caveat on the one above, because it is the part that a reader will otherwise skip. 'There are human studies' and 'there is human evidence for this use' are different statements, and the distance between them is this claim. Uncontrolled studies of a condition that fluctuates — interstitial cystitis, knee pain — cannot separate a treatment effect from regression to the mean, from the procedure itself, or from expectation. The knee study gave some patients two peptides, so even its uncontrolled result cannot be attributed to this one.
claims.uncertaintyText: All three were read at abstract level. A full text might report design detail the abstract omits; it cannot supply a control group that was not there.

evidence.interpretation: The abstract states that the material was manufactured by a 503A compounding pharmacy, that all twelve participants had failed prior treatment, and that the outcome was a self-rated global response after a single procedure.

The abstract states that the study was retrospective, that follow-up varied, that patients were asked to rate their pain by telephone, and that no specific tools were used to measure function, quality of life, stiffness or activities of daily living.
evidence.populationModel: Seventeen patients, some given BPC-157 with thymosin beta-4.

evidence.interpretation: The review classifies the studies it included as level IV and level V evidence, and reports that no clinical safety data were found.

claims.claimText: Every one of the twenty-two references the practitioner handbook cites for its BPC-157 entry is preclinical or a review. Twenty-one resolve to records in this screen: fourteen animal studies and seven reviews. The twenty-second, the only citation given for inhibition of tumour cell growth, is a 2004 conference abstract in a human melanoma cell line that is not indexed in PubMed.
claims.plainLanguageText: The handbook that clinics most often use for this compound lists twenty-two scientific references. None of them is a study in people.
claims.interpretationNotes: This is the crosswalk between what a practitioner source says and what it cites, and it is the most useful single fact this index holds about BPC-157. The handbook is not misrepresenting its sources: it says throughout that the findings are from laboratory studies, and it is accurate. What the crosswalk establishes is that a reader following its citations will not arrive at human evidence, because there is none at the end of them. Every mechanism in the entry — angiogenesis, nitric oxide, growth-factor signalling, neuroprotection, cardioprotection, gastroprotection — traces to work in rats, mice or cells.
claims.uncertaintyText: The crosswalk matched references by title against the screen rather than by identifier, because the handbook gives no PubMed identifiers and its bibliography is reproduced from an imperfect scan. Two references are near-duplicates of each other, which the matching preserved rather than merged. The melanoma abstract could not be located in PubMed at all, which is a statement about PubMed's coverage of conference proceedings as much as about the reference.

evidence.interpretation: The handbook's summary states that the healing effects are reported 'in laboratory studies' and carries superscript references 49 to 57 for them.
evidence.populationModel: Not applicable — a statement about what the source cites.

evidence.interpretation: The entry's statement that BPC-157 inhibits the growth of several tumour cell lines carries a single reference, to a 2004 item in Melanoma Research at pages A14–A15 — an abstract supplement — reporting work in a human melanoma cell line.

claims.claimText: As of 2026, independent reviews report that BPC-157 has no approved formulation, no validated dosing regimen and no completed Phase II clinical trial, and that it is not approved by the FDA or other regulators for absence of sufficient clinical study.
claims.plainLanguageText: No medicines regulator has approved this compound, and the reason given is that the clinical research needed to assess it has not been done.
claims.interpretationNotes: The previous version of this record could say only that the sources held here reported no approval — an absence in a small library. Two independent 2025–2026 reviews, one of them searching patent databases and regulator websites as well as three literature databases, state the position directly. That is still secondary evidence: a review saying a regulator has not approved something is not the regulator saying it. But it is a considerable advance on silence, and it is checkable.
claims.uncertaintyText: No regulator's own record has been consulted for BPC-157. The approach that produced authoritative labelling for tesamorelin — querying the FDA's own interface — returns nothing for this compound, which is consistent with the reviews and is not the same as confirmation from the regulator.

evidence.interpretation: States that the compound has not been approved for use in standard medicine by the FDA or other global regulatory authorities, owing to the absence of sufficient and comprehensive clinical studies confirming health benefits in humans. Also notes that it was temporarily prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency in 2022 and, as at the review's writing, is not currently listed.
States that the compound lacks FDA approval and that its use is banned in professional sport, while being increasingly used by clinicians and athletes.

notYetSupported.statement: That BPC-157 produces any effect in humans.
notYetSupported.why: Three human studies were identified by the screen of 13 September 2026, and none of them is capable of establishing an effect. All three are uncontrolled: two participants given intravenous infusions, twelve women treated in a single procedure with outcomes self-rated afterwards, and a retrospective telephone survey of seventeen patients, some of whom received a second peptide as well. A study without a comparison group cannot separate what a treatment did from what would have happened anyway, and the conditions involved — interstitial cystitis, chronic knee pain — are exactly the kind that fluctuate.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: A randomised controlled trial. Nothing smaller answers this question, and the existence of uncontrolled studies does not narrow the gap.
notYetSupported.researchQuestion: Does BPC-157 produce any measurable effect in people, in a trial with a comparison group?

notYetSupported.statement: What proportion of an orally administered amount reaches the circulation intact.
notYetSupported.why: Two sources report an oral amount and neither reports a bioavailability figure or a pharmacokinetic study. For a fifteen-residue peptide this is the question that determines whether an oral route delivers anything at all, and nothing held here addresses it.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: A pharmacokinetic study comparing oral and parenteral administration, in any species, reporting plasma concentrations of intact peptide.
notYetSupported.researchQuestion: What proportion of an oral amount of BPC-157 reaches the circulation intact, and how does that compare with injection?

notYetSupported.statement: An effective amount, frequency or duration for any purpose.
notYetSupported.why: Three sources give three different regimens and none cites a study establishing any of them. This index does not average regimens and does not choose between sources, so it has no amount to state.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: A dose-finding study, or any source that states the basis for the amounts it recommends.
notYetSupported.researchQuestion: Is there any amount of BPC-157 at which a measurable effect appears in people, and does the effect change with the amount given?

notYetSupported.statement: The safety profile of BPC-157 in humans, including with prolonged use.
notYetSupported.why: One identified study measured safety endpoints in humans: two people, three days, a panel of blood tests, no adverse effects reported. An independent systematic review searching three databases to June 2024 states that it found no clinical safety data at all. Nothing here addresses repeated use, long-term use, interactions, or use in anyone with a condition.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: Human safety data from a trial or a registry.
notYetSupported.researchQuestion: What harms occur in people given BPC-157, including with repeated and prolonged use?

notYetSupported.statement: Whether the compound's effect on blood-vessel growth is a hazard in cancer, a therapeutic possibility, or neither.
notYetSupported.why: Two research groups disagree about this in print, and the screen shows that neither side rests on human evidence. The concern is raised from mechanism in a 2025 literature and patent review; the counter-argument comes from the group that produced most of the preclinical work. The practitioner handbook's anti-tumour statement traces to a single 2004 conference abstract in a melanoma cell line, and its cancer-cachexia statement to a review that explicitly writes before any clinical trial.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: In vivo tumour model reports read in full, which would establish what was observed in what model at what exposure; and, for the clinical question anyone actually has, a study in people with cancer, which does not exist.
notYetSupported.researchQuestion: Does BPC-157 promote or inhibit tumour growth in a comparable in vivo model, and at what exposure?

notYetSupported.statement: The regulatory position of BPC-157 in any named jurisdiction.
notYetSupported.why: Two independent 2025–2026 reviews state that no regulator has approved the compound and give the absence of sufficient clinical study as the reason. That is secondary evidence and this index records it as such: a review reporting a regulator's position is not the regulator. The FDA interface that supplied authoritative labelling for tesamorelin returns nothing for BPC-157, which is consistent with the reviews and is not confirmation from the regulator.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: A statement from a named authority in a named jurisdiction, with a date.
notYetSupported.researchQuestion: What position has each named medicines regulator taken on BPC-157, and on what date?

notYetSupported.statement: What the laboratory studies behind every mechanism on this page actually did and found.
notYetSupported.why: Both practitioner sources cite their primary literature by superscript or by a link to the author's own website. None of those citations has been obtained or opened by this index.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: The primary publications, obtained and read, with each mechanism checked against the paper reporting it.

notYetSupported.statement: The inflammatory bowel disease trials reported under the development codes PL 10, PLD 116 and PL 14736.
notYetSupported.why: A 2006 review states that the compound was "safe in clinical trials for inflammatory bowel disease" under those codes, attributed to Pliva, Croatia. No report of any such trial appears in the 230 records the screen returned, and a 2026 review of the compound's development position states that no Phase II trial has been completed. The assertion is therefore either about trials that were never published, or a characterisation this index cannot check. It is recorded as a lead, not as evidence that trials happened and not as evidence that they did not.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: A trial report, a registry entry, or a regulatory submission under any of those codes.
notYetSupported.researchQuestion: Were the inflammatory bowel disease trials reported under PL 10, PLD 116 and PL 14736 conducted, and what did they find?

notYetSupported.statement: What the full texts of the three identified human studies report.
notYetSupported.why: All three were read at abstract level through the NCBI interface. Full texts are behind publisher access and have not been obtained. An abstract carries design, setting and size reliably; it does not carry the detail that would let anyone judge how the outcomes were collected.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: Access to the three full texts.

notYetSupported.statement: What the material used in the identified human studies actually was.
notYetSupported.why: One study names a 503A compounding pharmacy as the manufacturer and reports no characterisation of the product; the others describe none. Every quality question this index documents elsewhere — identity, purity, content, endotoxin — is unanswered for the material those participants received, which limits what even a well-designed study of it could have established.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: A certificate of analysis or product characterisation reported in the study, or an investigational product with a defined specification.
notYetSupported.researchQuestion: What do products sold as BPC-157 contain, and what was the material given in the identified human studies?

routes.populationModel: Not specified. The source gives amounts without describing a population or citing a study.
routes.formulation: Injectable solution; the source records an available 2 mg/mL, 5 mL presentation.
routes.limitationsNotes: Reported by a practitioner handbook as the route it recommends. No pharmacokinetic data, no bioavailability figure and no study establishing this route appear in anything held here. Recording a route is not a statement that it is appropriate, effective or safe.

The source gives an oral amount and nothing else. Whether a fifteen-residue peptide survives gastric and intestinal proteolysis in any useful proportion is the question this route turns on, and no source held here addresses it. The oral route is recorded here because a source reports it, and it is the least supported route on this record.

routes.populationModel: Animal alkali-burn model; species not specified by the source.
routes.limitationsNotes: Reported in an animal model only, for a specific injury type. This is the only route on this record for which the source describes an experimental context rather than a recommendation, and it is also the route with no human report of any kind.

protocols.objectiveContext: General use and injury-specific use, as framed by the Peptide Handbook.
protocols.regulatoryContext: Practitioner-described practice from a handbook. There is no approved product for BPC-157 and no regulatory assessment in anything this index holds. Not approved labelling, not a study regimen, and not a recommendation by The Tides Index.

disagreements.topic: How much BPC-157, and how often: three sources describe three different subcutaneous regimens for overlapping purposes.
disagreements.plainLanguageText: Three books describe three different regimens for the same compound, and none of them says what that is based on. This index shows each one attributed to the book that reported it rather than combining them into a single figure.
disagreements.explanationNotes: The differences are not obviously explained by population, route or formulation, because none of the three sources specifies a population and two do not specify a formulation. What distinguishes them is the framing: one is a clinical handbook, one a consumer book citing its own website, one a set of worked personas. The most economical explanation is that no source is working from a dose-finding study, because this index holds no evidence that one exists.
disagreements.resolutionRequirement: A dose-finding study in any species, or any source that states the basis for the amount it recommends. Absent either, this index will continue to show three attributed regimens and no recommended amount.

positions.positionText: The Peptide Handbook gives 300-600 mcg subcutaneously daily for 30 days for general use, and 300-500 mcg twice daily where the use is injury-specific.
Optimize Your Health with Therapeutic Peptides gives a single recommended amount: 250 mcg injected subcutaneously twice a day.

The Complete Guide to Peptides uses 500 mcg daily in its joint and tissue repair example, and 250 mcg twice daily in its skin repair example — two different amounts within the same book, for different stated purposes.

disagreements.topic: Whether BPC-157's effect on blood-vessel growth is a reason for caution in cancer or a reason to investigate it against cancer. Two research groups disagree in print, and a practitioner handbook carries both positions in one entry.
disagreements.plainLanguageText: This compound affects the growth of blood vessels. Tumours need blood vessels to grow. Some researchers treat that as a reason for caution in anyone with cancer; the group that has done most of the research argues that the compound regulates vessel growth rather than simply increasing it, and reports anti-tumour effects. This is an open scientific disagreement, and this index does not settle it.
disagreements.explanationNotes:
The screen makes the shape of this disagreement clear. A 2025 literature and patent review raises tumorigenesis as a speculative concern arising from the compound's pro-angiogenic activity. The research group that has produced most of the preclinical corpus published a comment rejecting that reading, arguing that the compound is angiomodulatory rather than pro-angiogenic and reporting prominent anti-tumour potential in vivo and in vitro; the reviewed authors replied. The practitioner handbook carries both sides without noting that they are contested.

What the screen adds is the weight behind each. The pro-angiogenic finding is supported by an animal and cell study showing increased vessel density in a chick membrane assay, restored blood flow in a rat hind limb, and VEGFR2 upregulation in human endothelial cells. The handbook's anti-tumour statement carries one citation: a 2004 conference abstract reporting inhibition of cell growth in a human melanoma cell line, not indexed in PubMed. Its cancer-cachexia statement traces to a 2018 review that proposes the application and says in terms that it is writing before any clinical trial.

So the two sides are not symmetrical in evidence, and they are also not resolvable from what exists: a cell line is not a person in either direction, and neither position has human evidence behind it.
disagreements.resolutionRequirement: A study in humans with cancer, which nobody has done. Short of that, the in vivo tumour models themselves, read in full rather than through a conference abstract and a review — which would establish what was actually observed, in what model, by what route, and at what exposure.

positions.positionText: "Although BPC-157 is angiomodulatory, use with caution in cancer and other conditions where angiogenesis may need to be suppressed."

The same entry states that the compound avoids VEGF-tumorigenesis, inhibits the growth of several tumour cell lines and can counteract tumour cachexia — citing, for the first of those, a single 2004 conference abstract in a melanoma cell line.
A 2025 literature and patent review raises the compound's pro-angiogenic activity as a possible route to tumorigenesis, as a concern arising from mechanism.

The principal research group's published comment rejects that reading, arguing the compound controls angiogenesis rather than simply promoting it, and asserting prominent anti-tumour potential in vivo and in vitro.

regulatory.indicationContext: No approved indication is recorded by any source held here.
regulatory.authority: None. No source held by this index is a regulatory source for BPC-157, and none names an approving authority.
regulatory.notes: Recorded as 'not approved' on the basis that three practitioner handbooks — two of which name brand names and manufacturers for other compounds, including in the same volume — record none for BPC-157. That is consistent with there being no approval anywhere; it is not the same as a regulator having said so. This index holds no regulatory document for this compound and cannot state the position in any named jurisdiction. The date is the date the sources were read.

forms.chemicalForm: The pentadecapeptide GEPPPGKPADDAGLV. No salt or counter-ion is stated by any source held here.
forms.molecularFormula: C62H98N16O22, as printed — the held copy is an imperfect scan and the subscripts are partly illegible.
forms.weightBasis: The peptide as such. No source held here states whether the figure is for a free acid, a salt, or a specific supplied form, and nothing about the material sold under this name is established by it.
forms.notes: Corroborated independently: a 1999 review identified by the screen gives the same sequence with a molecular weight of 1419, and a 2006 review repeats it. What a molecular weight does not establish is what is in any particular vial — which for an unapproved compound with no characterised product is the question that matters.
